blocks.p: The message from Okada Shizuka came early, before seven. It was one line long. It asked him to come back to the small white room at the Directorate that morning, and it did not say why.

Rei walked. It was already hot. The heat in Tokyo in August does not wait for noon. It comes up out of the pavement as soon as the sun clears the roofs, and the air is so wet that shirts stick to backs within a few minutes. He went down the long slope toward Ōji with the cicadas screaming in every tree. A woman was sweeping the step of a small house and had set out a dish of cucumber and aubergine on a little shelf by the door, with chopsticks pushed into the vegetables like legs. Rei knew what they were. They were the spirit horse and the spirit cow that families make at Obon. The cucumber is a fast horse, to bring the dead home quickly. The aubergine is a slow cow, to carry them back again with no hurry at the end of the week.

At the bottom of the hill the station was busy with people leaving the city for the holiday. Asukayama park rose green beside the tracks, loud with insects. Rei crossed in front of the east exit, past a vending machine glowing with cold green tea and canned coffee, and in one minute he was at the grey block that looked like a tax office. He had walked past it his whole life without looking up. Now he went in through its doors again.

Okada Shizuka was waiting for him in the same small white room as before. She was an assessor, one of the people who measured mediums for the Division, and her name was on the panel list by the door of the intake room. This time there was no laminated card on the table. There was only a single printout on thin, shiny thermal paper, curling at the edges the way thermal paper curls when a warm hand has held it too long. She did not slide it across to him. She laid her palm flat on top of it, as if the words might escape through the ceiling if she let go.
"The cycle ran Thursday," she said.

Rei felt the day land like a dropped stone. He remembered what she had made him promise, without quite letting him promise it. Do not let them assess him on a Thursday. He understood now that the warning had never been only about Gin.
"You weren't on the schedule," Okada said. "Sena flagged you anyway. The instrument reaches for whoever's nearest when a reading goes deep, and you were in the building."
She turned the sheet over. The strange thing on it was not a number. It was a shape.

Before he could understand the shape, Rei had to understand what the machine was drawing. Every spirit and every demon feeds on one register, one of the thirteen great feelings, the one that was strongest in it at the moment it died. And a living medium's gift leans toward one or two registers too, the way a singing voice has a natural key.

The assessment machine drew a medium's registers as a pair of rings, one inside the other. An ordinary citizen came out as clean round circles, one inside the next. A person with a fever of the veil came out as a fat smeared oval. Rei's rings were neither. His were two rings that should have been quiet, and instead both of them were leaning toward a third mark that did not belong to him. It was a faint bright knot off to the north of the page, like a moon that had wandered into the wrong sky.

"The textbook word for this is domain incipient," she said. She said it very evenly, the way a doctor gives a diagnosis she has decided not to be frightened of yet. "It means the machine thinks something is being built inside you. Or that something has already keyed in, and is reading you the way you read everyone else."

The sounds of Obon came faintly through the building's tired air conditioning. Out by the intake desk, paper lanterns sagged on their strings, hung for the dead who were meant to come home gently this week. Rei thought of the third mark, and of how it leaned north. Toward Kita. Toward a wall someone was patiently thinning.
Okada watched his hands, the way she had the first day.

"I have eleven hours before the cycle closes and the reading becomes a record," she said. "Once it's a record it goes up. To the Auditors. To the families above Adachi. To anyone who can act on a domain forming inside a registered medium. And what they do to a domain that's forming is close it. Early. While it's small enough to close."
She lifted her palm off the page at last.
"So. Before it's a record, it's still just a thing two people in a white room are looking at. What do you want it to be?"

blocks.cap: The Internal Affairs and Audit floor

blocks.p: The way down to the machine ran through Internal Affairs and Audit, the department that watches the Division's own people. Okada touched her badge to a door with no sign on it, and the noise of the building dropped away behind them.

It looked like the dullest room in the Directorate. Cabinets. Computer terminals. Very little talking. A plant on a windowsill that someone remembered to water. At the far desk a man in his thirties sat reading a file, with his tea going cold beside him. He did not look up when they passed. But Rei had the uncomfortable feeling that he had been seen anyway, completely, by someone who was watching the whole room instead of the people in it.

blocks.cap: Moriya Tatsuki, sixteen years in Internal Affairs

blocks.p: "Moriya," Okada said quietly, when they were past. "Sixteen years in Internal Affairs. He runs this floor. He's one of the good ones." She paused. "Gin used to say that's exactly why the floor frightened him. A good man with the power to file is still a man with the power to file."
Next to Moriya's office was a second desk, bare. No photographs. No papers. Only a fountain pen, old and expensive, laid square to the edge of the blotter with great care.

"That's Sena's," Okada said. "His father's pen. He doesn't use it anymore. Someone keeps it straight for him." She did not stop walking. "He has the Tower seat on this floor. The Auditor's chair that belongs, by an arrangement nobody wrote down, to a family."
"Which family?"

"Fujiwara-Kage." Okada said it the way people in the building said all seven of those names, Tsukishiro, Fujiwara-Kage, Orimoto, Higashiyama, Kuroda, Akiyama, Nishimura. Politely, and a little lower. "They're an investigation house. Edo. Their founders worked alongside the shogunate's intelligence men, and they've been reading people for the state ever since. Clairsentience runs in them like a family nose. They turn out Arbiters the way other families turn out lawyers."
Rei knew the name from Itsuki's photographs of Gin's Tower chapter. He had not expected to walk past one of their desks.
They waited for the inner lift. Okada kept her voice down.

"Of all the Tower families, they're the one most deeply inside this building. Two of them work here in senior posts. One in the Research Division. One in the Auditor network. Whether that's cooperation or infiltration depends on whose interest is being served that week. Probably both." Her mouth tightened. "The Grid says the family has been quietly documenting the Directorate's classified work for forty years. I've never been able to prove it. I've never tried very hard."
"And the Directorate lets them."

"The Directorate needs them. Gin will have written the whole arrangement down somewhere. The short version. They give it rank and training and cover, and it looks the other way, and a Tower child who joins us rises faster than their number earns." The lift came. "When I say the families above Adachi, that's who I mean."
Later that night, at home, Rei would find the page Gin had written about this family, in the chapter on the Towers. It was short. It said more than it seemed to.

doc.title: From Gin's book. Chapter Sixteen. On the Fujiwara-Kage.
lines: The Auditor network member from the Fujiwara-Kage, I know who it is and I am not naming them here.
My bi-monthly assessments are conducted by a different assessor than the one assigned to my district on the rotation schedule. I noticed this approximately two years ago. I have not raised it.
It may mean nothing. It may mean something that benefits me. It may mean something that does not. I continue to pass the assessments and I continue to note the irregularity.

blocks.p: The machine lived two floors further down, behind a door marked with nothing but a cycle number. The room was colder than the rest of the Directorate, on purpose. It was the cold of a place built to keep something still.

Rei had expected a machine with lights and dials and boxes that go ping. There was a machine. It was a low ring of grey instruments set into the floor, like a drain. But the thing the machine read through was a person. A young man sat at the centre of the ring with his hands open on his knees. His eyes moved, but they were not looking at anything.
Okada said his name the way a person names a place they are sorry about.
"Sena. Fujiwara-Kage Sena. He was a reader. A good one. Arbiter grade, two clean registers, the kind the Directorate doesn't get to keep as a witness. So they didn't keep him as one."

Rei understood before Okada finished, because he saw it the way he saw everything. Where a person should be, there was only a held breath. They had hollowed Sena out, gently. They had emptied his two registers until nothing of his own was left to colour a reading. So whoever the machine pointed him at came back true. Each reading was measured against a surface with no opinion of its own. He was the most honest instrument in Tokyo, because there was nothing left in him that could lie.

"He consented," Okada said. The sentence cost her something to carry across the cold room. "Eight years ago. Terms in his own hand. He thought it was service. His family thought it was a seat. The form doesn't have a box for what it actually is."
Sena's eyes found him then, slowly. For one moment something moved behind them that was almost recognition. It was the way a still pond moves when a fish turns, far below the surface.
"Gin's off-rotation assessor," Rei said. "For two years. It was him."

Okada did not answer, and that was an answer. She took a laminated sheet from a pocket by the door and handed it to him. It was the checklist every registered medium went through every two months, the one they were told was routine.

doc.title: Bi-Monthly Assessment Protocol. What Is Checked
lines: Stability profile. Current floor and ceiling against the registered baseline. Flagged if the floor has dropped more than fifteen percent from baseline, or the gap between floor and ceiling has narrowed. The most common flag.
Ability profile consistency. Verifies the registered type is still accurate. The instruments read against the standard single-path taxonomy. Capability outside it reads as instrument noise.
Register bleed. Emotional material picked up from heavy entity work. A grief-heavy caseload leaves grief in the signature.
Possession and cohabitation check. Assessors read for the double-layer signature of possession or cohabitation. Not disclosed to practitioners.
Behavioral review. Case history, supervisor report, flagged incidents. The most subjective part.

blocks.p: Under the fourth line, someone had written in pencil, in a hand Rei knew. The check catches entities that do not know what to hide. It does not catch entities that do.

"He passed every one," Okada said. "Clean. Before the fourteenth and after it. A thing that has studied a man for long enough knows what the assessment is measuring. It sits in the chair and gives the instrument what the instrument expects. A clean file doesn't mean he's uncompromised. It means whatever's in him is either absent or good enough at this. The file can't tell you which."

When the machine woke, it did not ping. It tightened. The cold in the room drew inward toward the ring. Rei felt his own two registers come half awake against his will. He had kept them pressed flat his whole life. Now they reached toward the empty young man at the centre of the room, the way water runs to the lowest place.
This was the reading that had flagged him, run again live. On the machine's grey panel the rings opened up once more. His two, leaning. And the third bright knot, to the north.

Now that he was inside the reading, he could feel what the paper could only draw. The knot was not inside him. It was reaching for him, from a long way off, from a direction he knew. It was patient and fond. And it had a familiar feeling that he would have recognised anywhere, because it was his brother's. It wore that feeling like a borrowed coat. It was not Gin.
Then Okada showed him the thing she had always known she would have to show him. He could not decide what the reading should become until he knew it could become anything.

The machine kept a calibration log. It was a record of every small adjustment ever made to keep the instrument accurate. She scrolled it back, past his Thursday, past months, to a column of small corrections that were not really corrections at all.

"The families above Adachi don't delete readings," she said. "Deleting leaves a hole, and holes get noticed. They recalibrate. They tell the instrument the honest answer is the error and feed it a kinder one, until the kinder one is what the machine believes."

Rei looked at the column and understood. The most honest instrument in Tokyo had been taught to lie so many times that lying had become a second language for it. This was how a possession became a footnote in a file. This was how a brother became a case closed too fast.
"You could do that to mine," he said. It was not a question.

"I could. Tonight." Okada did not look away from the screen. "By morning the machine would believe you're a fever-case with a bad week. No Auditor would ever come down those stairs looking for you." She let that sit. "And the one reading anyone has ever taken that shows what's wearing your brother would be gone. I'd have done it with my own hands. You'd have stood here and watched me learn how."
"Then leave the reading. Give it a different cause." He heard himself reaching for it. "Festival bleed. Contamination from a witness. Something boring."

"Then it's bent." She said it gently, the way she might have told him a bone was broken. "A reading you bend once never lies straight again. You'd never trust it after. Not even the part of it that points at Gin."
"And if nobody touches it at all?"
Okada was quiet for a moment. The machine ticked in the cold.

"Then it goes up. Up means the Auditors. What the Auditors do to a forming domain is close it early. Close you. Close whatever's reaching through you." Her voice stayed level, but her hand had found the edge of the panel and was holding it. "And they will not be gentle about which of you they decide is the patient."
Behind her, in the ring, Sena's open hands had not moved. But his head had turned a few degrees, toward the north. Toward the same wrong moon.
Rei looked at the column of kind lies for a long moment. He thought of Gin passing every assessment, clean, while something sat inside him and smiled at the instrument.
"Let it stand," he said. "It's the only true thing anyone in this building has written about him. I'm not going to be the next person who corrects it."
Okada closed her eyes for a second. Then she nodded, and she did not touch the log.

They came out of the reading room into a corridor where the Obon lanterns had begun to come down. The festival was closing. The dead were being seen back out. And the building was quietly going back to pretending it had never crossed over to them at all. Whatever the machine now believed about him would walk out in his file ahead of him, into rooms he would never see.
Okada walked him to the main lift and did not press the button. On the panel beside the doors, one floor had no number. It had only a key slot. Rei looked at it.

blocks.cap: Containment and Reintegration, where a closed domain goes

blocks.p: "Containment and Reintegration," she said, following his eyes. "That's where a closed domain goes. The cells. They call it rehabilitation, and they say it gently. The staff are kind. They bring the contained tea and learn their names and mean the word care. And they still close the door. Entry is by order, not request." She was quiet for a second. "Gin walked that corridor once. He told me he counted the doors he didn't open, and he still hadn't decided if that was cowardice or mercy."
"Is there anywhere in this building that sees everything?" Rei asked. "Besides him."

"One room. I've never been in it. I've only had it described." Okada kept her eyes on the shut doors. "The Mirror Room. Surveillance. A long dark room with mirrors hung in rows to the ceiling, each one showing a slice of the city from a height no person stands at. The operators don't talk. They drink tea and watch through birds' eyes and write down what the city is feeling. They're on no roster I've ever seen. It never closes. Two people I trust have stood in it, and neither wanted to talk about it for long." She breathed out. "Between that room and this one, the building watches the whole city. It just doesn't always know what it's looking at."
Then she said what she had brought him to the lift to say.

"Gin knew this would happen. Not the details. The shape. A Thursday. An instrument. You in the building. A reading that points the wrong machine at the right truth. He spent his last free act trying to keep you off this page. And you've spent the morning deciding to be on it your own way."
The lift came. Neither of them stepped in.

The morning had handed him one more thing, and it was heavier than the reading. Sena had turned north. Twice now, Rei had watched the emptiest person in Tokyo lean toward Kita, the same way his own registers leaned. A hollowed-out instrument has no homesickness of its own to explain that. So the thing that was reaching for Rei through the machine had been reaching through Sena too. It was testing every open surface in the building, patient and fond, wearing his brother's feeling like a coat.

The knot was not waiting for assessment day. It was using it. Every reading cycle the Directorate ran was a door the thing could prop open. The one institution that could close the wall in Kita had been holding a smaller door wide for years, without ever knowing it.

"I can put one thing in the record before it locks," Okada said quietly. The lift hummed behind its shut doors. "A flag of my own. I can mark the array compromised. Pull Sena from the cycle. Blind the Directorate's truest eye, and give your brother's reaching nowhere to land for a while. Or I leave him in. I leave the door propped, and we keep the one instrument that ever told us the truth, knowing exactly what's using it to find you."
She looked at him the way she had over the laminated card on the first day. She watched his hands more than his face.
"You've already decided what the page says. This decides whether the building keeps its eyes open, or shuts them to keep us safe. I won't make this one alone."

Rei thought of Sena's head turning, a few degrees at a time, toward the same place his own registers leaned. If they pulled him out, the thing would go quiet in this building. And they would lose the only window that showed it moving.
"Leave him in," he said. "If it's using him to look at me, then he's the one place we can watch it looking. Keep the eye open. I'll be careful what I let it see."
Okada held his eyes a moment longer. Then she reached past him and pressed the button, and the doors that had been open all this time finally began to close.
The lift rose through the building in silence. Somewhere around the third floor, Rei's phone buzzed in his pocket.
He knew before he looked. The name at the top of the screen was his brother's.
You looked tired today, Rei. Go home and sleep. Please.

He had not told anyone where he was going this morning. He had not been anywhere today where a person could see him. Nowhere except a cold room two floors under the street, with a ring in the floor and a hollowed young man at its centre, turning his head toward the north.
